utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. We're still sitting, as we were yesterday, pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I'm afraid it was impossible for us to sit again yesterday after we rose, for logistical reasons, court preparations for the following case, and it wasn't sure at that stage what the arrangements might be. We're very grateful for a lot of people changing their arrangements so that we can sit this morning in this court until 10.00. Mr. Hayden, what, if any, time would you want for re-examination in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: At this stage, no more than five, six minutes, as it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If we say 10 at the outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Karadzic, in that case, you have from now until 9.50. It is impossible for us to sit after 10.00 because we're being followed immediately by another case that's already been adjourned to allow us this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Excellencies. I appreciate very much this time that we have been given. And I see that we will be forced to seek to have this witness come back again, depending on the probative value of the paragraphs of his statement. May I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, as expeditiously and as quickly as possible, please, Mr. Karadzic, consistent with the interpreters being able to keep up, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Thomas, good morning.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 65 ter 9597 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Mr. Thomas, I just wanted to say I looked over what we were doing yesterday, and I wanted to assure you that I had no intention of insulting you or underestimating your rank. I just want us to get to the actual state of affairs in the best and fastest possible way. I'm not in any way contesting you; only just your views, some of them. 9597. I don't think it's been admitted yet in this case. I would like to tell you that this is an order for defence of the B and H Army, 1st Corps, of the 25th of October, 1993. Already, you were there. We're talking about the Muslim Army, an order for defence, from which we can see what they are doing and planning. Let me ask you this, Mr. Thomas: Do you know who held which positions around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't got the document, Your Honour, shown on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Nor have we yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer, in general terms, Dr. Karadzic's question: I had a general idea of the positions around Sarajevo, but we did not have a completely clear picture of the front-line, and that was only achieved after the cease-fire, when we were permitted access to the entire front-line, as I've stated in my statement. We did not have a complete picture of the front-line until the cease-fire, after which time we actually walked the cease-fire line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We still don't have the document, I'm afraid, in e-court in our system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just -- Dr. Karadzic, can you just put that to one side for a moment, until this problem is resolved, and go on with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that in one of your paragraphs exactly what you said; that until 1994, there was a war between the parties there, and there were no grounds for you to lodge protests because of the conduct of the sides because it was war. But then after a more serious cease-fire, probably after February 1994, then you had the opportunity to assess the actions and to protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We now have the document before us. Do you, sir, have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We're on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Thomas, to look at this document. We can see that this is from the 25th of October, 1993, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, that Croatian Muslim part, and this is an order for defence. In the first sentence, it states: "The city of Sarajevo is surrounded by the aggressor forces of the strength of a reinforced core." And then at the bottom, it says, this part that's underlined: "Anti-aircraft weapons are used as anti-personnel weapons. "Main forces are grouped in directions of Hadzici-Brezovaca," and so on, "from which they tie up our forces and are preventing their manoeuvring." Would you agree that this is a legitimate use of the artillery, this way that we were perceived by the other side? In the transcript, it is missing "artillery from which they are tying up our artillery forces and preventing their manoeuvres." Do you agree, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the point of -- where it says that their artillery forces are being used. It says anti-aircraft weapons are used as anti-personnel weapons and that they are supporting combat actions with artillery attacks. That's consistent with military tactics. What is your question relating to? I'm not sure what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then the problem is in the translation. You can see -- I'm going to read from it says here, "from which hold up our forces and prevent their manoeuvre," but in the original it says "from which their artillery fire is tying up our forces and preventing their manoeuvres." This is the fourth line of second paragraph of item 1, and you can see the villages of Rajlovac, Vogosca, Vilic, Mrkovici, Krupac, Vojkovici, Gornji Kotorac ...: [In English] "From which they hold up our forces and prevent their manoeuvre." [Interpretation] You are correct, the translation is missing, "using artillery forces to hold our forces and prevent the maneuvering of the same." In the Serbian version, you'll see the toponyms: "... Rajlovac, Vogosca, Mrkovici, Krupac, Vojkovici, Gornji Kotorac, from which the auxiliary forces are occupying the dominant buildings in the corps's area of responsibility, from which they are heading up our forces with artillery fire and preventing their manoeuvres?" Now, if you trust the interpreters, that they interpreted me correctly, would you then agree that this was a legitimate use of the artillery?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say that use of artillery to support combat action to delay or impede manoeuvre is, in fact, legitimate use of artillery. It's only when there's collateral damage on civilians that we begin to question it, or whether there's no military forces manoeuvring in an area, that we question the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, with all due respect, I would like you to stick to my questions and two documents. There is no mention of civilians here. Our enemy is not saying that we are misusing artillery against civilians. Quite to the contrary, they're saying we're using artillery forces to prevent them in their manoeuvres, which is legitimate. And then it says in the following sentence: "According to our knowledge so far, the aggressor uses the elderly and women to hold their positions, and young men, special (military and police) forces, volunteers from Serbia and Montenegro, and mercenaries," which there were none, by the way, "for offensive combat action. They start with forceful artillery attacks, followed by armoured equipment ...," and so on and so forth. Mr. Thomas, this is a document of the Muslim Army, and it describes what we were doing, as their enemy. It doesn't mention civilians anywhere. It says that we are using our last forces, the elderly, and women to hold our positions because we don't have any other forces, and we are using artillery to engage their forces and to prevent their manoeuvring. So would you please state whether you think this is a legitimate use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated, use of artillery to support defence is a legitimate use. And I also would like to point out to Mr. Karadzic that this is a military document. I agree with that, and the military document concerns itself with military activities. Probably some other organisation, certainly the Civil Affairs and the politicians on the Bosnian side, did tell us about the civilian casualties. And if you were to present another document in evidence, which it would no doubt outline all the civilian casualties from artillery fire. But this is a military document, and, quite correctly, they are only dealing with the things that interfere with their movement, their attacks. And if you are not familiar with the use of military documents and how we limit what we say in them, I suggest you listen to one of your military advisers. I'm sorry, Your Honour, to digress, but I don't like being asked a question on a narrow document which ignores all the other documents that exist in the realm of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the question was fairly focused. What Dr. Karadzic really asked is: Was it legitimately-used artillery, as it were, to proceed an infantry offensive. I'm summarising it greatly. And your answer to that was: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. I said -- I said yes it was, the first time, and I fail to understand why I got asked the question a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas. I'm not going to respond to this broadening of the issue, but I am disputing that we targeted civilians. So that is also stated in this document. Can we look at the third page of this document, please. Until then, I would like to draw the attention of everyone that the documents before items 5, the commander of the 1st Corps describes what is in each of the areas of responsibility, referring to different toponyms, Brijeg, Vis, and others, and issues assignments as to what they are to do. And then in item 5, it says: "The Croatian brigade --" 5.6, it says: "The Croatian brigade Kralj Tvrtko was organising a decisive defence in the area bridge over the River Miljacka, Hrasno-Vrbanja Most intersection, Djuro Djakovic, Marsala Tita, Elektroprivreda," and so on. This is the axis along which this commander is deploying the Kralj Tvrtko Croatian brigade, which is acting within the 1st Corps. And it says that the command post is at the Alija Aljagic School. Did you know about this and did you report about this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about this, and in one of my report sitreps, you'll see that a visit was made by one of my team leaders to the Croatian brigade headquarters, one of the sitreps that was submitted in evidence. We certainly knew where all the brigade headquarters were, and that was part of the routine of a military observer team is to visit on a daily basis, as is also stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is axis, which is the responsibility of the Croatian brigade King Tvrtko, is along the Miljacka River and is located in the very centre of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the urban, built-up area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we will look at 5.7, where it says, about the 15th Mountain Brigade, that it is going to be in the zone of the Miljevici, exclusive village zone, Colina Kapa, Vrbanja Bridge, City Hall, with the task of using convenient buildings as advantage points, and so on and so forth. Would we agree that this is 15th Mountain Brigade covers the part of Trebevic, via Colina Kapa, up to the Vrbanja Bridge? So from the hill, it is descending into the valley down to the river; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please recall that Colina Kapa is one of the peaks on the northern side of Trebevic, and it is to the south of the town?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When something drops from Trebevic on the town, Mr. Thomas, would you agree that it would be necessary to establish which hill it is coming from, whether from the one that is under the control of the Bosnian Army or one that is under the control of the Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in a position to do so, but not all the time, with the limitations that I made in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this refers to the number of men and also the freedom of movement of your personnel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I dealt with the lack of freedom of movement of both Serbs and Bosnians. Both parties denied us movement. In your case, I'm only talking about restrictions that your army imposed on me. If there was a Bosnian in your place, I would talk about his restrictions on my movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But for -- in order to be able to establish the objective truth, we need to know what the actions of the other side were. Would you agree, Mr. Thomas, that the lines on Trebevic were sometimes just 20 to 50 metres apart?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, in the red building, as I again have stated in my witness statement, the red building, the lines were only separated by a wall, and people were shooting through the wall. So I know how close the lines were because I, myself, was in that building. And I can tell you people poked holes in the walls and shot at each other. Yes, the lines were very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that the Muslim side held the actual peak of Debelo Brdo and the slopes facing the town, while the Serb side held the foot of the hill and the other side? Do you know where Debelo Brdo is?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at a map to refresh my memory, but I do have an idea of that general area. And I'm not convinced that we're talking about the tactical situation as it was throughout my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many men are in these brigades in the center of Sarajevo, how strong they are, and how large of a manoeuvring space do they need to be able to deploy according to the instructions in this order?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what the instructions in the order and what was actually on the ground, I think, might be at slight variance. I think they were limited in the number of resources they had available to actually man the front-line and keep a secure perimeter. So I think since you had this document, I'm sure your intelligence sources also knew that most of the Bosnian forces would be grouped very close to the front-line, because they didn't have the resources and the mobility to move further away from further away. So if you point out that there is defences along these -- in this built-up area, I'm suggesting to you that the positions that were occupied would be as close as possible to the front-line so that any incursion could not get a lodgement, and they would require most of the available manpower to do that. So you would know from -- if you had this document, you would know exactly where their positions were, and you would be able to direct artillery fire exactly on the locations where they had gathered their forces. And in some cases, in our observation, you did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, let's stick to the questions. According to your knowledge, what was the strength of the brigades in the center of town? We referred to a number of brigades that were deployed in these areas. What was the strength of those brigades?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I did not believe the data that was given to me by the Bosnians, and we had a very difficult time to estimate how many people they would have. And from our position, we would estimate what you call a brigade might only be actually a battalion size in a NATO standard. In fact, I suspect that you probably know better than we do the exact size because of your intelligence and informative networks in the city, so you knew how many people were in the Croatian brigade and you knew how many people were likely to desert. So I feel, Your Honour, that I'm being pushed into answering questions which he actually has the answers to already, because he's presenting a document which is obviously obtained through intelligence that has very detailed information about the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Major Thomas, you can't assume that this document was available to the Serbian forces at the time of the conflict. A lot of documents have been produced and disclosed thereafter. Secondly, what knowledge Dr. Karadzic might have is not evidence until it comes through you as an answer to a question, which is why he must ask you these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise, Your Honour, for taking up his valuable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, would you agree that it was your job to know the ratio of forces and to know what the strength of the forces in Sarajevo was? So the question was simply this: Do you know the average strength of a brigade in such a narrow area? For example, the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade or any other brigade, what was the strength of each of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- in the submission I gave yesterday, there is attached a document with strengths, as we suspected, of the different units. And if that hasn't reached Mr. Karadzic, I suspect that he is already aware of that information. But we had an estimate, and I would doubt -- I would doubt that even that estimate that was submitted yesterday from day to day would be accurate. And if you want me to go to my notes and -- I will look up the submission I gave yesterday and I will look up what the figure that was submitted on the Croatian brigade, if you want me to take the time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say you have notes there with you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a copy of the submission that I gave to the Court yesterday, and that submission -- I can't remember all hundred pages of evidence. And in that submission is a document that relates to what was estimated to be the strength of these brigades when I took over Sector Sarajevo. And if Your Honour would allow me leave to look at that, I can answer him from the document that was submitted, or he can wait and look at it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's already in documentary form. Then it would be a waste of a limited amount of time to do that. And perhaps Dr. Karadzic's team can investigate that. But can I just ask this, as a supplementary matter: Was it your impression that the Croatians were over-estimating or under-estimating their strength in their reports to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it depended on what the context was, but I would say that they probably over-estimated. I never considered any of the brigades to be a brigade-sized formation. I would consider them to be normally battalion-sized organisations, roughly. But depending on the leader and the area and the enthusiasm, a couple thousand people. But, of course, when there was a threat this could be supplemented by more people. But my impression was that they had a difficult area to hold, and that they did not want anybody to get into it, and that they would have been -- put their troops forward. But we were not allowed access to see their front-line positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the English? You see 5.8 there. 5.8: "The 2nd Mountain Brigade has the following line of responsibility: Kozija Cuprija, Hladivode, the City Hall, the Cathedral with certain tasks, and the command post is in Vase Miskina Street, the Foreign Languages building." Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you know, there were over 10 brigades in the inner-city of Sarajevo. As you said a few moments ago, from a couple of thousand to a full complement. So do you agree that it was between 50.000 and 80.000 men, soldiers who were able-bodied and who could function?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree that the force was that large or number of effectives. I don't think everyone had weapons. I think they had people rotating through the positions and picking up weapons that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also have General Halilovic's report to his own Presidency. If we have enough time, we're going to show it. Look at the 105th Brigade: "Linking the Museum of Revolution, the Sipad building, Trampina Street, and the command post is in Trampina Street, right by a big park where the Dom Milicije is, the very centre of town." Further down: "Hrasnica," and so on. Can we now have a look at paragraph 6. It's the next page in Serbian and in English. Do you agree, Mr. Thomas, that within town there was between 42 and 64 kilometres of a front-line; in the beginning of the war, 42 kilometres, at the end of the war, 64 kilometres of a front-line, where the two warring parties were directly facing each other?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps faced the 2nd and 3rd and 4th Corps along 240 or 250 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that, I don't agree. My main area concern and my main area of interest was either Gorazde, Zepa, or the perimeter of Sarajevo. The other responsibilities of that corps, I was -- I was not able to get access, nor could I have the resources to patrol. So I'm only interested in where you confronted the -- my main area of interest was where the -- your corps confronted the corps based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we are going to see on your maps that you did have an observation post to the north, towards Vogosca, and patrols in the municipality of Ilijas. Can we have a look at paragraph 6. Is that right, between Sarajevo and Vogosca you had a Papa observation post -- no, Lima observation post, and you had Lima patrols in Ilijas, at the very north of this area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only after the cease-fire, when a road was opened from Visoko to Vogosca for transit by the Bosnians to their other encircled area. We had no resources to patrol that area consistently during the conflict in Sarajevo, itself, so those patrols all started after the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We often come across this information that there was not enough manpower. What would have been sufficient resources for you to have sufficient insight all over?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the cease-fire was put in place, I was given up to 200 military observers. By June 1994, I was down to 60. As I handed in in this statement, I tracked a number of military observers that I had throughout my period there, and also the location of OPs which changed from time to time. I had a peak of 23 observation posts. At other times, I was down to only five or six. And it's all -- I prepared this briefing for senior officers in Zagreb, but it's equally useful to Dr. Karadzic, Your Honour. And it's also attached as part of my witness statement. And the resources -- the resources actually conceal a big deficiency that every 30 days we rotated people out. So during the two days of rotation, half of my complement of military observers might leave, and the new ones would be replacing them, and they would take time. And the priority during the first -- up until February was to monitor fire into the city and the fire units of the Serbs. And the patrolling was secondary. And at some times I even complained about not having enough resources to adequately man my responsibilities in Gorazde and Zepa, and those are -- also some of that is evident in the documentation I handed with my witnesses statement on the sitreps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please just tell me how many people you would have needed to cover everything and to know everything that was happening within your mandate. Could you just respond to that? How many people did you need for all of that? Nothing more than that, just how many people.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no military commander ever thinks he has enough people, so I could -- can't really answer that question. I thought that I had -- when I had 200, I was doing a good job, but it turns out I didn't know some of the things you've just told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have a look at paragraph 6 now. We see here that it says "Fire Support." This is a document of the Muslim Army: "Fire support. "Core artilleries in the Igman area. Observation posts in the areas of Mojmilo and Svabino Brdo." All of them are hills in the very centre of Sarajevo. You know where Mojmilo is and you know where Svabino Brdo is, right? Thank you. So: "Fire should only be opened within the defence area only on orders from the corps commander. "The firing post in the area of Zmajevac, Gazin Han, Bistrik, Mojmilo, Dobrinja, Hrasnica, Igman, Vitkovic, Svabino Brdo, Zuc, Buca Potok, Hum, Breka. "Firing positions N," I don't know what N means, "of the brigade artillery in the areas of Velesic, Sedrenik, Hrasno, Aneks, Butmir, Orahov Brijeg, Sip, Buca Potok." Are you familiar with these locations, and am I right if I say that all of this is within the inner-city, the area that we were surrounding? Just say yes or no. I don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, it says: "Observation posts in the areas of Svabino Brdo, Zuc, Hum, Grdonja, Zmajlic, Colina Kapa and Mojmilo." Do you agree that all of these were elevations that were held by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 7 speaks of anti-armour combat, and it says that: "The focus of anti-armour combat should be in the axes of Lukavica-Dobrinja, Ilidza-Stup, Rajlovac-Zabrdje, Vogosca-Hotonj, and Hresa-Borija. "Anti-tank for Red Arrow should be in Otoka, anti-armour launching positions in Mojmilo, Svabino Brdo and Zuc areas." Podrije [phoen] and Hrastova Glavica areas, that's where the anti-armour launching positions should be. Do you agree that this is an impressive force that we have surrounded, blocked in Sarajevo, itself?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think observation posts necessarily mean -- and they didn't detail the actual artillery resources that would be used. I stand by the intelligence summary that I gave that was attached as my witness statement. This is a nice-sounding order, but if the artillery observers don't have any resources to fire or they don't have stocks of ammunition to use, then it may not mean much. And, similarly, anti-tanks, they're talking about launching positions. That could be launching a missile, anything from a hand-held anti-tank weapon system up to a sophisticated vehicle-mounted one. We saw no evidence of vehicle-mounted anti-tank systems. So this is -- again, the order says one thing, but whether they had the capability on the ground is another thing. And as I have already submitted, the start point --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you. We can see here what -- from where they are going to fire. Observation posts are also on elevations. They are not part of their fire strength, but never mind, let's move on. The next page now, let us see what the PVO is using. Next page, please. The end of paragraph 8, that is. The next page. The 1st LARD of the PVO should be used for a circular defence of Mojmilo and Golo Brdo, Zuc and Orlic areas, in co-operation with the ARJ of the PVO of the 1st Motorised Brigade, the 2nd V Motorised Brigade and the 101st Motorised Brigade." You are familiar with all of these locations referred to in this order; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the locations. Your Honour, I don't understand what a LARD is. Is there some problem with the translation? A LARD, the 1st LARD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume it's an anti-aircraft weapons system, but I don't want to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic, can you assist by going back to the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you're going to denounce me as an incompetent supreme commander, but I have no idea what it is. It is probably an abbreviation for a light artillery rocket, something. They're probably using some unit to fire at targets on the ground. Believe me, I don't know. I think the first word would have to be "light." The L stands for "Light," probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's probably as good as we're going to get it. Either that or it really does mean "LARD."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept -- I'm assuming that it's a light anti-aircraft weapons system of some kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think you were going to assist. No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I've lost now what the question was about this, except was I familiar with the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that this anti-aircraft weapon is being used against targets on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D633, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2391, please. I just have the English version. Since we were wondering a moment ago what it was they actually had and what they were using for firing from these positions, there is just this one brigade here, the 102nd Motorised Brigade, and they are reporting as to what they have, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. We have the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put to you what it is that we see here, Mr. Thomas. It says: "The 101st Motorised Brigade," and then it explains activities, and then paragraph 3 speaks of neighbours, who is on the right, who is on the left, in terms of their own units. The right-hand neighbour is the brigade artillery group of the 2nd Vitez Motorised Brigade in the area of Vitkovic Brdo, then a platoon of mortars, 120-millimetres, and a squad of 82-millimetre mortars. Zestika, a platoon of 120-millimetre mortars, and two platoons of 82-millimetre mortars. Zrak, that's a factory in the centre of city, near the TV station, a platoon of 122-millimetre Howitzers: "The left neighbour. "Brigade Artillery Group of the 5th Motorised Brigade on firing positions --" I'm actually doing a site translation from English: "... in the area of Dobrinja."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, he mentioned a platoon of 122-millimetre mortars inside a factory. I think my English says a squad, which is a difference. A platoon would indicate it was a formed troop of up to four, whereas a squad indicates, perhaps at the most, two Howitzers. And inside a factory indicates not a firing position. But I'm glad he's enlightened me on where they were actually located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, I read it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, what's the question? Are you asking the witness whether or not he accepts the veracity of the information in the document? Because if he does, then that's probably enough for you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll accept that information. Some of the details, like the fact that those 122-millimetre guns were inside a factory, indicates why perhaps we never spotted those particular weapons. But, otherwise, I accept that . And they do -- I stand corrected. They did have some artillery inside the city, although I still stand by my statement that they didn't actually use them; from inside the city, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But over here, it's the 102nd Brigade that is reporting to the effect that they were, indeed, using that, and it was in this action that took place on the 1st of February, 1994, while you were still there. So we do see all of this. The 105-millimetre Howitzers in paragraph 4, and then in paragraph 3 we see: [In English] "Artillery group, 101 Motorised Brigade on firing position in the area of Mojmilo Hill, squad of mortars, 120 --"

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not reading anything that says these were fired. I'm still on a thing that's just outlining what equipment is there, and it's dated the 1st day of February. But I haven't got the screens that shows me that these things are firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What are you reading from, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the English translation, page 1. It says "Neighbours." You have it there, "Right neighbour, left neighbour." [In English] 3.2 and 3.3, "Brigade Artillery." And point 4, "[Indiscernible] Group 102." [Interpretation] What you have on your screen, Excellency, is the first page, it is the neighbours that are referred to here and what they have anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What's your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this kind of fire-power of the 101st Motorised Brigade, and did you report about it? I'm sorry, the 102nd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reported on the mortars. As I've just indicated in my previous statement, we were not aware of the 122-millimetre. And as you just previously stated, you said in this report it stated that it was firing, and I'm looking at this report and I see nowhere that it says the 122-millimetre artillery pieces were actually firing. And you, yourself, indicated that the Zrak squad of Howitzers was in a factory, which is a very poor fire position, so I'm just interested in whether we missed something and that these Howitzers were actually firing. And the 122-millimetre isn't normally a Howitzer; it's a gun. So perhaps they were not that -- didn't know what artillery they actually had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page, please, just to see what they have in terms of tank and anti-tank equipment. This is the 102nd Motorised Brigade in the area of Mojmilo and west of Mojmilo. Do you see number 5 "Anti-Tank Combat": [In English] "The focus of anti-tank combat should be on the following directions: Azici-Stup, Market Street-Refrigerated Warehouse, Kasindolska Street-Stup, Nedzarici-Stup, Energoinvest-Stup. "Anti-tank squad composed of: Tank squad of T-55, APC M-60s, squad of infantry combat vehicles M-80," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] And 5.1: [In English] "Tank squad of T-55 is placed in the expected area of Brijesce Hill," and so on and so forth. [Interpretation] Just one brigade, Mr. Thomas, has this kind of power, and finally it was signed by the brigade commander. Actually, Hajrudin Grabovica, the chief of staff. So when he says where the anti-tank line is going to be -- or, rather, where this combat is going to take place, and he refers to Kasindolska Street in the Serb part of Nedzarici, you think that they just held that there and that they weren't firing from it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we never spotted them firing those tanks. And the other question I would have followed up after seeing this is whether all the brigades had this kind of fire-power or whether this is tanks being assigned to that brigade and that's why it's reading the way it is. It doesn't tell me, in fact, where those tank resources are located. One of them, it says it looks look they're starting from an area of a warehouse or something. So most definitely we did not see those tanks firing at that time, and we did report tanks, as -- again, in the statement I handed in, there is tanks firing later. So this is a piece of paper. We did not see the tanks fire. I think we would have noticed it because we were watching for when they would actually use weapons. And the limited number of tanks they had, we were very curious, Your Honour, about when they were going to use them. So to answer directly, Dr. Karadzic, we did not see these tanks fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was your task, Mr. Thomas. You should have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, if he didn't see them fire, the witness didn't see them fire. It doesn't mean to say they didn't fire. All he's saying is he didn't see them fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I might add the Serb people at the time on the front-line didn't advise us or complain about Bosnian tanks firing, either, or we would have investigated it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the reports of the Serb side, we can see how many casualties that the Serbian side has suffered from these weapons mentioned here. Can this document be admitted? We haven't really got much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 9491. Let's see what another brigade has, and then we are going to move on to some other topics. We are really short of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, it says here that this order is being issued by the 1st S. Brigade: "Wartime duties of the 1st S. Motorised Brigade, the armoured battalion, according to temporary wartime establishment, the command of the armoured battalion and the 1st Tank Company." When one has a tank company, doesn't that mean that one has tanks as well?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes. It doesn't mean that, in fact, it isn't a deception plan, it doesn't mean that they actually have the tanks with them or they aren't all destroyed or hidden away or whatever. We would have been very interested in the location of a company of tanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't read the -- there's no English translation, so I don't know for sure that this document refers to a company of tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The translation is being checked, as they say, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There is no translation available for this document, and I don't think the witness has been able to comment on it or verify anything in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No. The witness couldn't attest to this document, even though there's no dispute that the contents were accurately translated by Dr. Karadzic, so there's no basis for admitting it at the present time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, that says a great deal about the mission of the UN Military Observers. How can we take these findings into account of an insufficient service? 1D2396, could we have that now, please. S. Motorised Brigade again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make an observation at this point. I believe Sector Sarajevo, which included all the other units in Sarajevo who also had eyes on the front, none of them reported a tank company, either. For example, in that general vicinity there would be -- there were a French battalion, an Egyptian battalion, and nothing was reported by them either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, plainly, no military mission is going to be 100 per cent successful. But if you didn't see something, you didn't see something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the 1st S. Motorised Brigade Command, 4th of February, 1994: [In English] "The following officers are appointed to carry out its war duties in 1st S. Motorised Brigade, in mixed artillery battalion, according to temporary war formations." Do you agree that this mixed artillery battalion existed in this 1st S. Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring -- relating that to the previous document that I looked at, then I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please? Actually, we could admit both of them on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see what else is in this document. Is this the entire document, just appointing officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance here. We do have the original, and this is just a -- the translation on the screen is an extract from that original. So, at the very least, we would ask that the entire document -- two-page document is translated before admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D635, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the light of this new answer, can the previous document be admitted in the same sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hayden, logic would dictate that that's probably a wise course. We're talking about the document, rather than the truth of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We don't have any objection to the authenticity of the previous document. Therefore, no objection, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So that will be marked for identification as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Thomas, that on page of the transcript of the 15th of September yesterday, 6870, line 20 on, you replied to my question about reports by Victor Andreev, and you said: [In English] "I was aware of this memo. My second day in Sarajevo, I had no reason to believe it or disbelieve it. I didn't know the officer involved to prepare this memo, and I certainly don't believe paperwork that is handed in front of me ...," [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. Now I'm going to put a question, and it should be answered with a yes or a no. Was there antagonism and disagreement in the views of the UN Military Observer Mission and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at MFI D155. This is also a Muslim document, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Supreme Defence Staff, Security Administration, dated the 7th of December, 1993. Can we -- yes, this is the first page of the document. Can we look at page 3. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the Military Security -- Military Secret Service of the Muslim side, and in this part in the box it says: "In conversation with members of the UNMO which were visiting the areas of responsibility of the 1st Mountain Brigade and the 2nd Viteska Mountain Brigade, it has been learned that a large number of members of Chetniks formations are staying in Rajlovac with the markings different from those born by the so-called Army of Republika Srpska, even though it was banned before to wear such insignia. These UNMO members, in conversation, also indicated that there is allegedly antagonism between them and members of the UNPF, emphasising that they are informing their superiors in an objective way, but that the bulk of their information is being censored in the Zagreb Command, and information censored in this way is being sent to the UN. The possible disagreement between the UNMO and the UNPF in the Sarajevo area shows the expressed interest of members of the UNMO for information from members of our units that relate to criminal actions by members of the UNPF (black market, alcohol, drugs, prostitution)." Three questions, Mr. Thomas. Does the Serb side have any reason to be suspicious if your or anyone's members or mediators would inform the other side about what they see on our side; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because if any of my people were found transmitting information to the other side, they would be sent out of Sector Sarajevo. So if they did it openly or were caught, they would be gone. In fact, they would probably be sent home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do not dispute that that would be so. But if they are not caught, would the Serb side then have reason to be suspicious, and that is why they were reluctant to see international forces on their territory, out of concern that the other side would receive information? I'm talking about cases when they are not caught, just like these people were not caught.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an allegation which has not been substantiated. And, secondly, I can't do anything about people I didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, I think you were going to make a similar observation, I anticipate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I hope so. I'll wait to see what your observation was, but it may have passed us by anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, I mean, I was going to say, Dr. Karadzic, you're giving a hypothetical situation and asking the witness to speculate about it. I mean, what he says must be culled with common sense. If he didn't know somebody was doing it, he couldn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, the Defence believes that the secret report by the Secret Service of the Muslim Army is evidence that members of UNMO spoke with them, and in that conversation they relayed what they saw in Rajlovac. I'm not disputing and I do not doubt that Mr. Thomas would punish them, but that still doesn't mean that Serbs had no reason for caution. And this is evidence that our opponents were receiving information about our situation. This is what I'm talking about only. This is a Muslim document. The Secret Service established that the MOs were informing them about the situation in the Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My second question, Mr. Thomas, is: Is it evident here that you investigated these forces in relation to criminal acts? That is what it says here, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we did not investigate criminal acts. The UN had its own agencies for investigating criminal acts. Our responsibility was only to report it, and after that no further investigation. And if the -- if I'd been tasked to do it, I would have refused, because it was the exception of one or two police officers on call-out from the Scandinavian countries. None of my military observers were trained in police work. So I categorically say we did not undertake criminal investigations, and if we had or were made aware of criminal investigations, we would immediately report it to the appropriate UN authorities. And I can personally say that when I found at least one individual - I can speak without mentioning names - was involved in a criminal activity, I made sure he left the sector. Does this answer the question for the -- Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, of course, it's Dr. Karadzic's question, not mine. But what you're saying is this, if I can summarise it: If you found out or suspected somebody was involved in illegal activity, you would report it further up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the UN had established appropriate authorities to deal with that. They even had a police element.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that -- can we look at -- do you recall that the Ukrainian Battalion in the Krupac location was replaced because of smuggling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krupac location, I'm not aware of that. It doesn't -- was that -- I don't think that was located in Sarajevo. Was it? Are you talking about the Ukrainian Battalion area in Sarajevo, which was not on the front-line, down --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Krupac is next to the Famos factory in Hrasnica, and this is where Zoljas, Osas and -- were smuggled, and evidence was collected that even they carried rockets and bombs on stretchers, and the Muslim Army would buy weapons that would slip by us. And this is something that was found out by the United Nations, and then this smuggling of weapons to Muslims was stopped. Had we had time, we would have shown evidence of this, and we might do that on some other occasion. But were you aware of these matters?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, because -- I do know about Ukrainian smuggling, but we had no Ukrainian elements in Hrasnica during the nine months that I was in Sarajevo. The Ukrainian elements were based in the city proper, and a company was based in the Zepa pocket. So I'm not sure about what we are -- what was the time-frame we're talking about. There was an element of criminal activity certainly in Hrasnica, but it was associated with the Bosnians, not with the Ukrainians -- any Ukrainians that might have been there. My understanding, that was -- during my time was a French area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at -- this one was MFI'd before. Can we now look at 1D0346.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Thomas: In your statement that has over 120 paragraphs, we've seen that some documents that were shown to you and that were admitted, you interpreted them. Did the Prosecution ask you to provide your expert opinion on those documents, those reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of which documents, Your Honour, that the accused is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you're going to have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, I wouldn't have interpreted any documents from any other language but English, even though I do read French. So if there is an interpretation, perhaps you'll have to ask the Court officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean "translation" in that sense. I just meant an expert professional analysis, that type of interpretation. There are paragraphs here, for example -- it's a paragraph referring to documents. It's paragraph 96 of your statement, where you provided your professional expert opinion about numerous findings, sitrep reports. So did the Prosecution ask you to give your professional expert opinion about those findings and reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at my binder to see if those aren't some that are now been taken out because of -- is it dated after my time? Because I understand from the Prosecution's Office that some documents are being re-submitted. What is the date, Dr. Karadzic, of the documents you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your consolidated statement of over 120 paragraphs, so this is the last statement of -- or interviews from November 1997 and May -- and 2009, May 2009. And this is 65 ter 22787, and these are the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to save time, if I made a statement based on my expert opinion, that's what it would be, expert opinion. I underline the word "opinion." And if it's there, to save all the haroosh [phoen] of going back through all these documents and figuring it out exactly, it was an opinion based -- and I was presumably being asked to comment on somebody else's submission and to give the Prosecution's Office some idea of what it meant. Does this meet Dr. Karadzic's requirements or do I have to look up the specific document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: For myself, I don't think we have anything like enough time to pursue it in that detail at present. Dr. Karadzic, I mean, the statement appears to speak for itself, in the sense that it seems to be evident that the witness was doing what you have asked, he was providing an opinion about reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it has any probative value, an expert evaluation of documents by this witness, who is in the capacity of a witness here and not as an expert, then we need to kindly ask the Trial Chamber to have this witness recalled, because this is a very voluminous statement with many assertions that have to be tested by the Defence. Thus, practically the whole indictment relating to the Sarajevo area is contained in this ambitious statement and this ambitiously-conceived witness on the part of the Prosecution, so we need a week for this witness, not just a few hours. If we are taking it into account, then we have to ask him to come back and so that we can objectivise each of these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that isn't a matter which can possibly be determined at this stage in the proceedings. It is, of course, open to you to call evidence which challenges the findings of this witness. And, indeed, there would be little point in recalling this witness unless there was an objective and subjective challenge to each part of his evidence, backed up by other evidence, so it's something that needs careful consideration. Have you any other questions you can usefully ask now? I think we have time for one more before the Prosecution's re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more. I would like to call up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Thomas: You knew General Rose, is that right, and he commends you personally on page ERN 63 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Dr. Karadzic be asked to repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The UNMO reporters were completely useless." [Interpretation] He -- [In English] "It was a money-spinner. They wrote shoot -- shoot-reps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is R063-0106, page 4. [In English] General Rose: "The UNMO's reports were completely useless. It was a money-spinner. They wrote shoot-reps and reports based on what they were told by the local commanders. Many were not technically competent, and some were sold out."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this comport with what you were saying, that we were not informing you that we were being shot at, and had we informed you, that you would have reported about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that statement. I don't know whether that, in fact -- I don't have a copy of that document in front of me, so I don't necessarily believe that even General Rose even said that. But I can tell you that my people observed the shots -- fall of shot that was reported, and they also reported the outgoing ammunition that was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Karadzic, that must be the last question. Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, a few brief questions concerning your cross-examination. Yesterday, Dr. Karadzic was asking you about Croatian or HVO fire on Sarajevo, and this is at transcript pages 85 and 86 of the uncorrected transcript. You said, at line 15 of page 85: "We do know that shells fell on the city from Croatian artillery, and that was identified and reported separately." Subsequently, Judge Morrison asked you about the frequency of that shelling, and you replied: "The only reason -- not very often." And you went on to say the reason you recalled that was an anecdote, you would tell people about the convoluted nature of the war in Yugoslavia. If I can call up 65 ter 10575, Mr. Registrar, which I believe is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been admitted as P1561.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: With respect to your comment about reporting Croatian activity, if we look down to paragraph 2(b), and we see each of the warring factions named, and the headline "Incident report, increp levels." Is that a reflection of the fact that each of the warring factions had their activities reported?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. However, this was a report that was designed for Zagreb, where obviously they were monitoring what the Croats did in other areas. And so in this case it would have been so unusual that we would have sent a special report. And, in fact, I'm not sure that UNMOs observed the Croatian fire, but it might have been, in fact, one of the -- probably the French battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: To follow up that answer: If I understand correctly, if Croatian fire into Sarajevo was observed, it would be reported in the daily sitrep or a report?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be reported in our report, yes. And so what I'm suggesting is that I don't recall it being necessarily reported by military observers. I suspect it -- since it fell in the Croatian area, the Croatian brigade area, and since the Croatian brigade area fell within one of the areas of responsibility of the French Battalion, it was most likely that report originated with the French Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you spoke about two specific sniping incidents that you recall, and I wanted to clarify something about each of those. The first one was at transcript page 47, and you discussed the death of an elderly man near a CNN vehicle. Do you know which side perpetrated that sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We could not determine which side killed this man. And it wasn't near a CNN vehicle. He was killed, and then the CNN vehicles passed by. And, of course, they stopped and did a public relations take on this or a news -- on this. So we could not determine who fired the shot, and we could not -- the only motive that we could attribute to this man being killed, because he surely did not look like a fighter, was that he had been killed so that CNN would record it for their news. And since it happened at 2.00 in the afternoon, we knew that it would make it back to North America in time for the CNN sound-bite at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You also spoke, Major Thomas, about an incident concerning a young woman, a 19-year-old woman, who you said was shot while speaking on the phone with her boyfriend. Do you know where she was speaking on the phone with her boyfriend when she was shot?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in an apartment building that overlooked Dobrinja. And I just happened to be in the area, and I wanted to see my patrol undertake this investigation. They had been requested to go there. And on that day, I was also visiting that particular area to find out -- to find out how they were managing dealing with the collection point of the bodies from the incidents. So I also found this -- I saw this young lady again with a different patrol, where they were -- and then finally I did the patrol at night. And it was the people at the scene where she was first hit that told me that they had recovered -- you know, the phone was still in her hand, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And do you recall what type of clothing she was wearing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was definitely in civilian clothes. Well, her leg had been sort of blown off, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Earlier today, Dr. Karadzic began to ask you about a paragraph in your statement, I believe it's paragraph 57 to 60, where you discussed protests that were made. Dr. Karadzic paraphrased you as saying, and this is at transcript page 3: "Before February 1994, 'no grounds for you to lodge protests because of the conduct of the sides.'" And if I can take you to paragraph 57, which I believe he was talking about, where you said: "Prior to February 1994, the sides were at war, so it was rather difficult to protest anything." Did the difficulties of protesting anything prevent you from making any protests?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we -- we certainly protest. And as Dr. Karadzic indicated, he didn't think it was the place of a major to talk to General Galic. So as I said in my statement, I was stonewalled by Major Indjic. So often, usually what would happen is the Egyptian colonel at UNPROFOR headquarters would prepare a note -- a formal note which would be couriered across to Lukavica, but, of course, we didn't feel that that was going to result in anything either. However, in cases of -- and just to clarify, when I talked about co-operation of local brigade commanders, when we had some casualty lying out in the open, we sometimes could arrange a cease-fire and time to get that individual brought behind the lines of either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And one final question. Yesterday, you were asked about paragraph 47 of your statement about the local agreements with Serb brigade commanders, and this is at transcript pages 67 to 68. When you said that Bosnian Serb brigade commanders were confident in making local agreements, generally speaking, what were the subjects of those agreements? What was the subject-matter?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied, depending on the time, but I certainly remember getting -- as the one in June 1994, where I was able to get the battalion -- the Bosnian battalion commander to stop his unit from retaliatory fire for a sniper incident, and I was able to get my three military observers out, where they were caught in no-man's land, where they had gone to try to rescue three Bosnian women. And I think I described that incident already to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And would those agreements affect matters outside the areas of responsibility of that brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No brigade commander on any side would talk for a brigade -- talk for another brigade commander's area. They wouldn't in our army, either. So they were very -- they were very -- nobody wants somebody else interfering in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are no further questions from the Bench. Major Thomas, it simply remains to thank you for coming to give your evidence on this occasion, and you are now free to leave. And a safe journey back home. The Court will now adjourn. The trial will recommence at 9.00 a.m. on Monday, the 27th of February, for the reasons which have already been given in public -- September. Now, we talk about Freudian slips. There's one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.04 a.m.,
